episode.broadcastScript:
Welcome to The Innovation Pulse from Innovating Higher Ed. It's Wednesday, March 4th.

As universities nationwide sign multimillion-dollar A.I. deals, writing educators just passed a resolution affirming something different: the right to refuse generative A.I. in their classrooms. The tension between institutional adoption and faculty resistance is getting interesting.

-
In our Ethical A.I. category today, Santiago Canyon College hosted award-winning journalist Karen Hao for a critical discussion about A.I.'s darker side. Hao, author of "Empire of A.I.," shared details about the exploitation of workers in Kenya who label disturbing content for ChatGPT training. Her book chronicles OpenAI's transformation from nonprofit to tech giant, raising questions about the human costs behind the technology we're rushing to adopt.

-
From the Latest A.I. Products file, Northwestern University is among institutions now offering dedicated artificial intelligence majors. The trend reflects higher education's response to A.I.'s expanding role across industries, though it raises questions about whether we're training students for jobs that may not exist or preparing them for a world where A.I. handles much of what these majors teach.

-
In our Insights and Trends category, a Metropolitan State University Denver professor is making a counterintuitive argument. As A.I. disrupts white-collar jobs, he suggests general studies programs may prove more valuable than specialized tech training. Critical thinking and communication skills remain durable, he argues, while technical skills become obsolete faster than ever.

-
And here's one worth watching from our Practical Tips category. A Babson College writing professor is exploring how to teach students when to struggle intellectually versus when to use A.I. tools. The challenge isn't banning or embracing A.I., but helping students develop discernment about what thinking can accomplish without technological assistance.

-
Now, let's get to that story I mentioned at the top about writing faculty pushing back against institutional A.I. adoption.

-
The Conference on College Composition and Communication just passed a resolution that's making waves across higher education. It affirms faculty and student rights to refuse generative A.I. in writing classrooms, even as their institutions sign major tech partnerships. This isn't just academic politics, it's a fundamental disagreement about what education should accomplish.

On one side, you have institutional urgency. Arizona State, Cal State, and University of Colorado have all inked major A.I. partnerships, framing these as essential for student competitiveness. When tech companies warn that A.I.-savvy graduates will have employment advantages, the pressure to act feels real. Administrators worry about leaving students unprepared for an A.I.-integrated workplace.

But writing faculty are raising compelling counterarguments. They point to A.I.'s environmental costs, data privacy concerns, and potential erosion of critical thinking skills that develop through the writing process. Their resolution argues that writing instruction serves purposes beyond workforce preparation, helping students navigate uncertainty, build community, and engage in civic participation.

The practical implications vary significantly by institution type. Community colleges face particular pressure here. With diverse student populations and workforce development missions, they're caught between preparing students for immediate employment and developing foundational skills. Yet community college students may benefit most from developing thinking and communication skills without technological shortcuts.

What's most interesting is how this resistance reframes the entire conversation. Instead of asking "How should we use A.I.?" writing educators are asking "Should we use A.I. at all?" They're questioning the assumption that technological adoption is inevitable, pushing back against what one professor calls "compulsory opt-in culture."

This movement reflects broader concerns about academic freedom and shared governance. When institutions sign sweeping A.I. deals without faculty consultation, they're making pedagogical decisions that affect classroom practice. Faculty report feeling pressured to integrate tools they haven't chosen and may not trust.

The resolution also challenges the efficiency narrative driving much A.I. adoption. Writing educators argue that some struggles are productive, that the difficulty of writing is often where learning happens. When we shortcut the thinking process, we might be solving the wrong problem entirely.

For community college faculty, this creates a particular tension. You're already stretched thin, serving students with varied preparation levels. The temptation to use efficiency tools is strong. But these writing educators are asking whether our rush to adopt A.I. tools actually serves students or just makes our jobs easier.

The resolution offers something valuable: permission to pause. It validates concerns about A.I.'s impact on student learning and suggests that opting out isn't backward-looking but thoughtfully principled. The question shifts from whether you're keeping up with technology to whether the technology serves your students' actual learning needs.

This isn't anti-technology sentiment. It's pro-learning advocacy. Writing faculty aren't rejecting innovation, they're insisting that pedagogical decisions should be made by educators, not tech companies or administrators responding to market pressure.

For educators making decisions about Monday morning's classes, this resolution provides cover for thoughtful resistance. It suggests that saying no to A.I. tools can be as professionally responsible as saying yes, depending on your teaching goals and student needs.

-
The writing faculty resolution reminds us that not all innovation serves learning. Sometimes the most innovative thing you can do is resist the pressure to innovate.

That's your Innovation Pulse for Wednesday. Find full coverage and links at innovating higher ed dot com. See you Thursday.

Dr. Norma Jones. Thanks for listening.
